source.title: Multilingual Sentence-T5: Scalable Sentence Encoders for Multilingual Applications
source.authors: Chihiro Yano; Akihiko Fukuchi; Shoko Fukasawa; Hideyuki Tachibana; Yotaro Watanabe

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are not available as text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether performance scaling extends to multilingual sentence-embedding models fine-tuned on NLI data, a different setting from language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size comparisons for downstream sentence-embedding benchmarks. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, compute-optimal allocations, or fitted power-law exponents. Other benchmark results that do not compare model sizes are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study compares three mT5 encoder sizes after NLI fine-tuning and reports downstream STS and retrieval performance, directly bearing on V6 in multilingual sentence embedding. It does not test a power-law functional form.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: they report a positive correlation between encoder size and sentence-embedding performance, call this scaling laws, and emphasise benefits for low-resource or English-distant languages. Their evidence establishes a size-performance trend, without fitting or validating a power-law form.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes mT5 encoders with NLI contrastive learning and query/value LoRA, and measures downstream sentence-embedding benchmarks. It does not fit the original studies' held-out language-model loss curves or evaluate compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Fine-tuning data affects results: the text reports XNLI as more effective for retrieval and en-NLI as more effective for XSTS. Evaluated language pair also affects the size-related gains; the authors note larger benefits for English-distant languages.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation
record.problems: Only three model sizes are compared; no power-law exponents, curve fits, or prediction errors are reported. The scaling measure is downstream sentence-embedding performance, not held-out pretraining loss. Table 4 reports no uncertainty estimates. Figure 2 values are not numerically stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying model-size outcome rows were left out. Other evaluation results were omitted because they do not compare model size.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law dependence on parameters, tokens or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Fitting small runs and testing predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
Fixed-compute optimisation and power-law growth of optimal parameter and token counts.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds beyond text pretraining; fine-tuning is studied, but no such functional form is fitted or tested.
Quantitative prediction of downstream scores, extrapolation beyond the three tested sizes, and prediction from pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: The sizes 564M, 1.7B and 5.7B refer to extracted mT5 encoders, not complete encoder-decoder models or trainable LoRA parameter counts. Comparisons between m-ST5 and other architectures, and LoRA configuration comparisons at one backbone size, do not independently test the listed scaling versions. No uncertainty estimates are supplied for the Table 4 size comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions evaluated against much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
No controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study tests size-related downstream performance in multilingual sentence encoders, but does not establish the same power-law form for loss or test other modalities, repeated data, or other training regimes.

The paper measures downstream sentence-embedding benchmark performance against model size, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or quantitative prediction of downstream outcomes from a fitted scaling curve.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across parameter-counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices; no curve bending is tested.

relationships.condition: XNLI fine-tuning, all five Table 4 language pairs, 564M to 1.7B to 5.7B encoders
relationships.reason: r1-r5, r11-r15 and r21-r25 show monotonic STS improvements at both size increases, supporting the directional scale-performance relationship.
relationships.display_finding: Semantic similarity scores increased at both size steps for all five language pairs.

relationships.condition: en-NLI fine-tuning, all pairs from 564M to 1.7B; all except es-es from 1.7B to 5.7B
relationships.reason: r16-r20 improve by 5.2–24.8 points over r6-r10; r26-r27 and r29-r30 improve by 5.0–8.1 points over their 1.7B baselines.
relationships.display_finding: Scores improved by 5.2–24.8 points at the first size increase and by 5.0–8.1 points for the specified pairs at the second.

relationships.reason: r28 gains only 0.4 points over r18 despite more than tripling encoder size, showing much weaker improvement in this setting.
relationships.display_finding: Performance improved by only 0.4 points despite increasing encoder size from 1.7B to 5.7B.

relationships.condition: Tatoeba-36 retrieval, overall size trend with XNLI and en-NLI fine-tuning
relationships.reason: For the comparisons represented by r31-r36, Section 4.3 and the introduction explicitly report a positive size-performance correlation; this verdict rests on that text, because individual figure steps cannot be verified.
relationships.display_finding: Retrieval performance reportedly correlated positively with model size under both fine-tuning approaches.
